item.title: seeking greenlight: ehe birh: Re: seeking greenlight: ehe birh
item.content:encoded:
I know mystery and unsolved questions are at the heart of the Foundation and its mythology but this one is just too vague. A bird that communicates with other birds and occasionally transform humans into birds is an interesting concept but I hardly see how it could create a end of the world scenario. It seems that you just want it to be dangerous and powerful but you're not giving me enough info to actually be afraid of it.
Either tone it down and make it more of an annoyance than a cataclysm, or put some effort into making it beliavably powerful. Also, think of the containment procedures and possible ways to counter the human-bird transformation.

item.title: A World Of D-Class: Re: A World Of D-Class
item.content:encoded:
It also means that The Foundation must make the best use of a limited resource, adding an additional layer of realism in what is an otherwise unrealistic universe.

That's part of the reasoning, the fact that the numbers cannot physically sustain the number of D-Class the Foundation uses. The fact is that death row inmates condemned to die from a western point of view are really the people that fit the D-Class narrative, and there is simply not enough of them.

Not only would you need to show that the people are indeed evil, but that they deserved their fate.

I feel like I can do that, the Foundation would never use an object without doing its due research.

There's also the question of whether or not they are viable test subjects. While there are a number of situations where you want explorers, there are also a number of situations where you want living subjects, simply because they would react as living subjects (such as how chemicals affect them as well as the natural respiration systems).

They function as a normal person in every way except that they've lived before, that's a part of the anomaly

item.title: SCP Idea: "Albularyo" (Seeking Greenlight): Re: SCP Idea: "Albularyo" (Seeking Greenlight)
item.content:encoded:
Hi, pal!
I am a newcomer so I can't greenlight it but I do have some questions and opinions about your article.

First off, I like the idea of mixing traditions/folklore with Foundation style anomalies and your idea really does it well. I was just thinking about why this specific Albularyo is kept under confinement and others aren't. Is it just because of its hostility? I understood that the Albularyos don't have the power to create curses, they just contact entities that can, is it right? If so, how would the Foundation react to these? Try to capture some? Exorcise them? Use them?
Your idea is really cool but I think it needs better interaction with the Foundation and its universe, think not only of this specific Albularyo but on all of them and how their existence affects the world and the Foundation. I hope this is useful feedback, if you want to discuss further I would love to.

item.title: Seeking Greenlight: Green Man's Chefs: Re: Seeking Greenlight: Green Man's Chefs
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

They are extremely hostile to living things, especially humans except for their human employees.

This feels like a weird outlier in your pitch; like…why are the SCPs chefs cooking for humans when they hate living things and especially humans? It feels to me that this'd be more effective if they like were over friendly or whatever and just really wanted to please with their meals whilst also being alien and not really getting that like…cooking a human kills the human?

and no one has seen the restaurant's kitchen. The restaurant shut down due to sanitary reasons.

This feels a little incongruous to me: generally a restaurant being shut down for sanitary reasons would be like cos the food storage is disgusting or something; and so like…need access to the kitchen to know?

Tests were made with various non edible materials and the resulting dish is reported to be delicious no matter what the ingredients were and how it was prepared.

I'm not really sure that it's worth putting this in the article; it feels…like it might just be quite info-dumpy.

I think on the whole, this feels…like a really interesting idea that just needs you to do something interesting with it? Like I think part of me really just wants a like, investigation log where a foundation agent goes in and orders food and just, experiences gradually weirder and weirder things until they finally break into the kitchen and discover some shocking secret about it before the piece ends, y'know? Or just…some sense of the Foundation doing something with like the capture chefs or the investigation that's interesting and not a vague nod to how it was found or w/e.

item.title: A Canary In The Coal Mine: Re: A Canary In The Coal Mine
item.content:encoded:
I didn't communicate it well, but Dr. Gables wants this researcher to get an SCP designation and he want whatever pay rise would come with it, so he wants the research data while expunging his own involvement in it.

Also him snapping was gonna be a build-up as the reader realises that this man has something weird going on. He would eventually reach the tipping point where he realises that he didnt consider if he got the cause and effect mixed up, aka. this researcher drinking a can of this soda wasn't a premonition but instead a trigger, and thus must be eliminated for 'the sake of humanity'.

The foundation, being a greyly moral organisation, can't deny the correlation and data even if it was collected in a way they wouldn't have done it in.

Do those details help clear it up? Or does the logic still seem weird? My only issue is why the foundation wouldn't lock up this researcher in case it is a trigger instead of a premonition. I though it might be funny to hand wave it away with a memo from the 'Department of Temporal Relativism' stating that 'In essence, they are both pretty much the same thing'

Thanks for the feedback!

Like there's kinda a progression through the logs with the events getting more severe and the foundation eventually changing track to try a different approach; but it feels…unguided? item.title: Greenlight request- Frozen Corpse and Nervous System: Re: Greenlight request- Frozen Corpse and Nervous System
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

I guess I'll explain what I can about the narrative; I wasn't going to, since this is only a brief initial pitch, but hopefully you'll find this to be interesting at least.

If you want greenlights on an idea, you have to pitch the whole idea and not just some of it.

My concern with the narrative here is that it feels…lacking in closure? It might work if you can get a reader to feel invested in the SCP and so it being frozen indefinitely ends up feeling like a huge sad moment; but it feels like it might be hard to land that in a way that works? Particularly since the freezing here is implied to be perfect (i.e., that they've circumvented the usual issues where ice shards form within a body and rupture the cells); and so in turn, there's an implication that even if they wait a really long time, they could still wake her up?

The other issue with doing a sad ending here is that it feels like it might be really hard to get a reader to emphasise with the legs here; like…it's not like they can really talk and be a character and so you're likely going to have to rely on characterising them via their actions and mannerisms.


I'm willing to greenlight this though because I don't think either thing here is a major issue, and I think it'll be easier to tell if it works via a draft y'know? This said: there's a possibility this might work best as a tale and I'd urge you to seriously consider that. It'd allow you to spend a lot more time in the researchers mind if this was like…a write up of that investigation happening and his reaction to stuff, than if like, he has to formally write it up in a SCP file, y'know?

item.title: Seeking Greenlight On My Idea: Re: Seeking Greenlight On My Idea
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

I have a multitude of ideas for these interviews which (as I haven't begun writing them yet) aren't super fleshed out, but have, what I think is, a good basis.

My concern with the ones you've listed out is that it feels like it's lacking a sense of coherence: they don't feel like they're building off each other so much as like, four completely separate interviews that could fit in any order.

I understand the "Native American curse" concept may be somewhat overdone

It is both really overdone and pretty problematic and I would urge you to not do this.

That said: the core story of the person here is the most interesting aspect of this to the point where I'd probably focus the story around like…what drove them to do this and how it gets wrapped and stuff; everything before this feels like a really lengthy preamble that doesn't add a tonne, y'know?

Everything after that in the log, will be mostly excluded/expunged, menial information (pH testing, and marking the times the fountains appear) as to avoid massive exposition.

I'd probably suggest not putting a tonne of menial information in this, or massive expunged sections: at the end of the day, you're wanting to write something interesting for a person to read and not a complete accounting on this.

An addendum will tie things up, from one of the interviewers, warning that further disruption of the phenomenon could be genocidal

This feels…overblown? Like, it's a relatively localised phenomenon and so it doesn't feel like this is a credible threat. But even if it did, having someone just kinda…say that this is the case feels like it'd be a really underwhelming way to show it?

I think my strongest advice is to focus this arc on the person who made it; and why they made it, and how like, the Foundations attempts to contain this/the person affect it's working. Like the angle of the foundation bringing him into containment and then the fountain killing a bunch of folk is interesting, particularly if we can kinda see the maker go through an arc where e.g. they realise they made a mistake here or something?

item.title: Intergalactic blackmail: Re: Intergalactic blackmail
item.content:encoded:
Okay so I have two big concerns here. The first is that narratively, it feels like this is very similar to SCP-4645 in style; down to the like, random blackmail claims and the unclear like, requirement for what the foundation should do.

The second is that this doesn't really go anywhere: you introduce the mystery of who is sending this and that the blackmail changes repeatedly but it doesn't go anywhere. Like, the foundation doesn't investigate who sent it, they don't really debate whether to accede to the demands, they don't refuse and have progressively worse things happen; so it just feels very…flat?

My advice: figure out how you can show why this is interesting. Figure out what the narrative arc of this is.
